trait_value_raw: attributes that seem to support the idea of a wind pollination syndrome
notes: 'The attributes that seem to support the idea of a wind pollination syndrome in R. sprengelioides are the smooth, dry monad pollen which is readily released as a pollen cloud from the terminal inflorescence, lack of nectaries and both the anthers and stigma are well exerted from the perianth, as the perianth falls off at anthesis.'

trait_value_raw: morphology and attributes ... support a similar situation [to R. sprengelioides]
notes: 'The morphology and attributes of R. procera which could be measured in this study support a similar situation' (i.e. the wind-pollination syndrome described for R. sprengelioides in the same paragraph).

trait_value_raw: a number of attributes that indicate it is likely to be wind-pollinated
notes: 'The Victorian species R. victoriana also has a number of attributes that indicate it is likely to be wind-pollinated, particularly the very high pollen:ovule ratio.'

trait_value_raw: grouped with the other possibly wind-pollinated richeas in Table 3, but flagged as unstudied/uncertain
notes: Most speculative of the four Richea candidates: 'Richea milliganii has monad pollen but is different from the other possibly wind-pollinated richeas in several other characteristics -- namely, the large pollen, presence of nectar and the pendulous, rather than erect, flowers. Unfortunately this species has not been studied in any detail and there are no observations on how it might be pollinated.' The source also raises an alternative hypothesis: 'Could R. milliganii be an example of an ambophilous (sensu Linder 1998) taxon with flowers initially receptive to buzz pollination with wind pollination as a fall back position?' Included here because Table 3 groups it with the other wind-pollination candidates, but this is the lowest-confidence call of the four -- flag for review.

trait_value_raw: considered to be definitely wind-pollinated (Schumann et al. 1992)
notes: 'Erica coarctata is considered to be definitely wind-pollinated (Schumann et al. 1992).' This conclusion is attributed by Ladd (2006) to Schumann, Kirsten & Oliver (1992), not derived from this paper's own analysis -- E. coarctata is used throughout as this paper's known-wind-pollinated reference standard for comparison, not a novel finding.

trait_value_raw: characteristics which could be interpreted as ambophilous -- freely shed pollen from well exerted anthers while still producing nectar
notes: Source describes E. labialis as ambophilous, not purely wind-pollinated: 'Similarly E. labialis has characteristics which could be interpreted as ambophilous -- freely shed pollen from well exerted anthers while still producing nectar' (also Abstract: 'E. labialis can produce abundant pollen when the plant is shaken but also produces nectar'). Recorded as the compound value 'wind biotic' since AusTraits' pollination_syndrome has no dedicated ambophilous/mixed-strategy term -- a modelling judgement call, flag for review.

trait_value_raw: tapping the stem would produce a cloud of pollen
notes: 'Field observation of flowering Richea sprengelioides showed that tapping the stem would produce a cloud of pollen.' Distinguished from the pollination_syndrome row above because this is a direct field observation (pollen visibly released under mechanical disturbance), not a floral-morphology inference -- though tapping is used here as a proxy for wind-induced stem movement, not literal observation of wind itself dispersing the pollen, hence 'possible' rather than 'known' vector.
